source.title: Gradient responsive regularization: a deep learning framework for codon frequency based classification of evolutionarily conserved genes
source.authors: Anjum Shahzad; Tahir Mehmood; Sheeraz Akram

record.file_problem: Full article text supplied; no truncation or garbling apparent in the provided text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests train–validation gap and associations with batch size, learning rate, gradient norms, and sharpness in trained MLP variants on genomic classification, using a different task and measurements from the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports separate train–validation gap ranges and qualitative observations on gradient norms and sharpness. Its model comparisons of GRR against regularization baselines are not themselves results about the listed versions. It does not test memorization of random labels, test error after widening past interpolation, image convolution versus fully connected architecture, optimizer generalization, or dropout effects.
record.test_reason: The study benchmarks regularization methods for genomic species classification. It does not measure the fixed-epoch batch-size effect in V5 or magnitude-aware sharpness versus generalization gaps in V7. Gradient norms and unscaled Hessian sharpness are treated as indicators of overfitting without establishing the claimed held-out-performance relationships. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' interpretation but understates their main conclusion: they claim GRR improves genomic classification over conventional regularization in selected configurations, especially learning rate 0.0001 and batch size 32 on the complete dataset, while achieving over 99% accuracy on both datasets. They interpret small validation gaps and smoother low-rate optimization as evidence of robustness. Their claim that complete-data gaps are tighter conflicts with the numerical ranges reported.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains MLP variants with gradient-responsive regularization for four-species codon-frequency classification, not the natural-image or language tasks and interventions in the versions. It reports batch-size and learning-rate analyses, but no fixed-epoch comparison of test error across batch sizes.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported gradient norm and sharpness patterns vary with learning rate, batch size, and dataset; larger batches particularly at higher learning rates are described as more variable or associated with overfitting tendencies.

fits_no_version.finding: Small aggregate train–validation accuracy gaps and differences in gap variability across genomic datasets and regularization methods.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MLP variants achieve near-perfect genomic species classification with small reported train–validation gaps under cross-validation and early stopping.

fits_no_version.finding: Higher learning rates, particularly with larger batches, produce more abrupt gradient changes and more variable Hessian sharpness; lower rates produce smoother trajectories and flatter solutions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning rate and batch size affect optimization dynamics and unscaled solution sharpness in genomic MLPs; these measurements alone do not establish generalization penalties.

record.problems: The study reports train–validation rather than train–test gaps for the gap analysis. Gap results are mostly aggregate or qualitative and do not isolate batch-size effects. The complete-data conclusion reports gaps of −0.008 to 0.006, while the Results section also discusses a peak gap of 0.006. Sharpness and gradient-norm evidence is described qualitatively; no numeric association with test error is presented. The paper notes that near-perfect metrics on RBH-filtered genes may reflect dataset bias and says the findings may not generalize beyond Poaceae.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. GRR and comparator test/validation classification metrics were excluded because these are regularization-method benchmark outcomes, not results measuring the claim versions.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting alongside natural-label generalization and chance-level held-out accuracy for random labels.
Test error after widening beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.

Held-out-performance penalties from larger batches under fixed epoch budgets and their recovery through recipe adaptation. Training uses early stopping; reported gap summaries do not isolate batch size.
The effect of adding or removing dropout. Dropout is included in the recipes without an intervention isolating its effect.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus generalization gaps among comparably fitted networks, including comparisons against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus removing equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Batch-dependent classification performance is discussed elsewhere in the text, including improved GRR test accuracy at batch size 128 on RBH data. These early-stopped genomic comparisons do not test V5's fixed-epoch image/language claim. Absence of an applicable measurement is not evidence that any version's effect is absent.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization are not tested.
No width sweep or test-error behavior around the interpolation threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected image classification comparison.
No comparison of adaptive optimizers with SGD for generalization.
No fixed-epoch comparison of large and small batches against test performance; no language models or training-recipe adaptation comparison.
No dropout intervention or comparison of dropout with augmentation.
Does not measure magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or compare it with norm- and margin-based generalization measures; sharpness analysis is qualitative and on genomic tasks.

relation.reason: The study discusses larger batches, sharpness, and generalization, but its reported results measure related constructs rather than the specified claim effects.

tranche.reason: The study benchmarks regularization methods for genomic classification. Its gap summaries and optimization indicators do not establish V5's held-out-performance penalty under fixed epoch budgets or V7's magnitude-aware sharpness relationship; no other version is tested.

source_check.notes: The paper calls complete-data gaps tighter and MLP/GRR fluctuations reduced, although its reported ranges and stability bounds are larger. Methods and figure captions also disagree on batch sizes; the relevant gap and dynamics sections use 32–256.
